title: Services and the three ports
summary: A stable address in front of pods that keep changing.

steps.title: Why Services exist
body: Every pod gets its own IP, but pods come and go: a rollout replaces all of them, and each replacement has a **new IP**. Clients cannot keep a list of pod IPs.
A **Service** is a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of *whatever pods currently match its selector*:
```text
Service shop-api  10.96.14.2:80
selector app=shop-api
(only pods that are Ready are listed)
The endpoints controller keeps an **EndpointSlice** listing the ready pods' IPs. kube-proxy on every node programs iptables/IPVS so traffic to `10.96.14.2:80` is spread across them.
```text
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=shop-api
Empty endpoints is the number one cause of "the Service doesn't work": the selector matches no pods, or none are Ready.

steps.prompt: A Service has no endpoints. Which is **not** a plausible cause?
options: The selector says `app: shop-api` but the pods are labelled `app: shopapi`
All pods are failing their readiness probe
The pods are in a different namespace from the Service
steps.explain: ClusterIP is the default and normal type. A Service only selects pods in its own namespace, and only Ready pods become endpoints.

steps.title: port, targetPort, containerPort
body: Three numbers that people mix up constantly:
```yaml
# Service
spec:
selector: { app: shop-api }
ports:
- port: 80          # what CLIENTS connect to on the Service IP
targetPort: 8080  # where the traffic is sent on the POD
# Pod template in the Deployment
containers:
- name: api
ports:
- containerPort: 8080   # documentation: the app listens on 8080
```text
client --> shop-api:80 --(Service)--> podIP:8080 --> app listening on 8080

`containerPort` is informational (the app listens wherever it listens), but naming it lets the Service use `targetPort: http` so the number lives in one place. If `targetPort` does not match what the app actually listens on, connections are **refused** even though endpoints look fine.

steps.prompt: The app listens on 5000. Clients should call the Service on 80. Fill in the numbers.

steps.title: Service types
body: | type | Reachable from | How |
| **ClusterIP** (default) | inside the cluster only | virtual IP + DNS name |
| **NodePort** | outside, via `<any-node-ip>:30000-32767` | ClusterIP + a port opened on every node |
| **LoadBalancer** | outside, via a cloud load balancer IP | NodePort + the cloud provisions an LB pointing at it |
| **ExternalName** | inside | a DNS CNAME to an outside name, no proxying |
Each type builds on the previous one. In production you usually expose **one** LoadBalancer (for the Gateway's proxy, next lesson) and keep every app Service ClusterIP.
A **headless** Service (`clusterIP: None`) has no virtual IP; its DNS name returns the pod IPs directly. StatefulSets use one so each pod gets its own name.

pairs: the orders service calls the payments service inside the cluster
quick test from your laptop on a bare-metal cluster: `node-ip:31080`
public IP on AKS for the Gateway's proxy pods
refer to `db.legacy.corp.example` by an in-cluster name

steps.prompt: A pod fails its readiness probe while the others pass. Endpoints only include Ready pods. What does this print?

steps.title: Fix a Service with no endpoints
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The `catalog` pods are healthy (`kubectl get pods -l app=catalog`), but nothing reaches them through the
Service: `kubectl exec shell -- wget -qO- -T 2 http://catalog/` fails.
Find out why with `kubectl describe svc catalog`, `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=catalog`
and the pods' labels and ports, then fix the **Service** (not the Deployment) so that the request answers.

checks.name: catalog has 2 ready endpoints on the app's port
checks.cmd: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=catalog -n default -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | .ports[0].port as $p | .endpoints[]? | select(.conditions.ready) | $p] | "\(length) ready on \(.[0])"'
checks.fail: The Service still has no (or the wrong) endpoints. Its selector must match the pods' labels, and `targetPort` the port the container listens on.

checks.name: a request through the Service answers
checks.cmd: kubectl exec shell -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://catalog/ | grep '^Name:'
checks.fail: `wget http://catalog/` from the `shell` pod still fails.

checks.name: the Deployment is unchanged
checks.fail: Fix the Service; leave the Deployment as it is.

hints: `kubectl get pods --show-labels` vs `kubectl get svc catalog -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'`: one letter differs.
`kubectl get pods -l app=catalog -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].ports}'` shows the container port (named `http`).
steps.explain: A Service is a selector plus a port mapping. `Endpoints: <none>` always means the selector matches no ready pod (a typo, a missing label, or pods that are not Ready); endpoints that refuse connections mean the `targetPort` is wrong. Naming the container port (`http`) and using `targetPort: http` keeps the two from drifting apart.

steps.title: Build it: a Service with no endpoints
prompt: Every request gets 503 although the pods are healthy. In the **Kubernetes builder**, find out why the Service has no endpoints and fix it.
steps.explain: A Service selects pods by label. One letter of difference between the selector and the pod labels means zero endpoints, and `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>` shows it.
